name: Decorator
intent: Add behaviour to an object by wrapping it, without changing its class and without a subclass for every combination.
scenario: A coffee shop sells espresso with optional milk, mocha and whip. Each add-on changes the description and the price, in any combination.
problem: Customers combine add-ons freely: milk and mocha, double mocha, whip on top of everything. Subclassing for each combination (EspressoWithMilkAndMocha...) creates a class explosion, and you still cannot build one at runtime.
solution: Give every add-on the same interface as the drink and let it hold another drink inside. Milk wraps an Espresso, Mocha wraps the Milk drink, and so on. Each layer calls the one inside it and adds its own bit.
pain: One class per combination: 3 add-ons already means 8 classes
Double mocha needs yet another class
Add-ons cannot be chosen at runtime from a customer's order
Price logic is copied across classes
benefits: One small class per add-on, combined however you like
The order is assembled at runtime from user choices
Each add-on's price lives in exactly one place
whenToUse: You need to add responsibilities to individual objects dynamically
Subclassing would cause a combinatorial number of classes
Extensions should be stackable and removable: logging, caching, compression, validation layers
whenNotToUse: You only ever need one fixed extension: plain inheritance or a method is simpler
Code depends on the exact concrete type, which wrappers hide
The order of wrapping matters in subtle ways and is hard to document
pitfalls: Debugging stack traces get deep: many small layers
Order sensitivity: wrapping in a different order can change the result
A wrapper is not the same object: identity checks and type checks break
Lots of tiny classes can be hard to follow without a clear naming convention

roles.label: Component
roles.description: The interface shared by plain objects and decorators.

roles.label: Decorator
roles.description: Base wrapper: holds a Component and forwards calls to it.

roles.label: Concrete Decorator
roles.description: Adds one specific behaviour before or after forwarding.

quiz.question: A coffee app has Espresso, plus decorators Milk, Mocha and Whip, all implementing Drink. An order arrives from an API as the list [milk, mocha, mocha]. How should the drink be built?
options: Create a class MilkMochaMochaEspresso for that combination ahead of time
Make Mocha extend Milk, so that one object covers both and a second Mocha adds another layer
Switch on the list and call a different factory method for each known combination of add-ons
Start from an Espresso and wrap it in the matching decorator for each item in the list
quiz.explanation: Because every decorator has the Drink interface and holds a Drink, they can be stacked in any number and order at runtime, so a loop that wraps is enough. Per-combination classes or factories need an entry for every possible order.

quiz.question: A price is built from a $10 base. A Discount decorator takes 10% off the inner price, and a ServiceFee decorator adds $2. What is the final price of ServiceFee(Discount(base)) versus Discount(ServiceFee(base))?
quiz.explanation: The inner layer is computed first. Discount then fee gives 9 + 2 = 11. Fee then discount gives 12 minus 10 percent, so 10.80. Wrapping order changes the result, which is why the order of decorators needs to be documented.

quiz.question: A client is built as Logging(Retry(HttpClient)). Later code does `if (client is HttpClient) client.setTimeout(5)`, and the timeout is never applied. What is the best fix?
options: Add setTimeout to the shared interface so each decorator forwards it inward
Make each decorator extend HttpClient, so the check passes and setTimeout runs on the outer layer
Compare the class name as a string instead of using a type check, then call setTimeout on the result
Check for the decorator base type and set the timeout on the outermost wrapper, which stores it
quiz.explanation: A wrapper is a different object, so type checks against the concrete class fail. Putting the operation on the shared interface and forwarding it down reaches the real client. Extending HttpClient or storing the value on the outer wrapper leaves the inner client's timeout unchanged.
